questions.stem: What is the definition of specific heat capacity?

options.text: the energy needed to warm 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
options.explanation: Per kilogram and per degree — the full definition.

options.text: the energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance
options.explanation: That describes latent heat of fusion, not specific heat capacity.

options.text: the temperature rise produced by 1 joule in any mass
options.explanation: The definition fixes the mass at 1 kg and the rise at 1 °C.

options.text: the total energy stored in a heated object
options.explanation: That is thermal energy, not a per-kilogram-per-degree property.

questions.stem: Which is the correct unit of specific heat capacity?

options.text: J/kg
options.explanation: That omits the per-degree part.

options.text: J/kg °C
options.explanation: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.

options.text: J/°C
options.explanation: That omits the per-kilogram part — heat capacity, not specific heat capacity.

options.text: W/kg °C
options.explanation: Watts measure energy per second, not energy.

questions.stem: Two identical pans, one water and one oil, sit on identical flames. The oil warms faster. Why?

options.text: the oil pan receives more energy
options.explanation: The flames are identical, so the energy supply is the same.

options.text: water always stays at the same temperature
options.explanation: Water warms too — just more slowly.

options.text: oil has a lower specific heat capacity than water
options.explanation: A smaller per-kilogram price means the same energy buys more degrees.

options.text: oil has a higher specific heat capacity than water
options.explanation: Higher capacity would make the oil warm more slowly.

questions.stem: Why is water used as a coolant in car engines?

options.text: its low specific heat capacity lets it heat up fast
options.explanation: Water's capacity is high, not low — and the cooling role wants that.

options.text: water conducts electricity around the engine
options.explanation: Pure water is a poor conductor and that is not the design goal.

options.text: water boils away to carry heat as steam
options.explanation: A coolant is meant to stay liquid, not boil off.

options.text: its high specific heat capacity lets it absorb lots of energy for a small temperature rise
options.explanation: High capacity makes an excellent energy carrier.

questions.stem: A hot sand beach cools within minutes after sunset while the neighbouring sea stays warm for hours. Which property difference explains this?

options.text: sand's specific heat capacity is much lower than water's
options.explanation: Low capacity swings temperature quickly both ways.

options.text: sand's specific heat capacity is much higher than water's
options.explanation: High capacity would make sand the slow one.

options.text: the sea receives extra energy at night
options.explanation: Both lose energy after sunset; the capacities differ.

options.text: water cannot cool below air temperature
options.explanation: Water cools freely; it just does so slowly.

questions.stem: State what a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C tells you about water.
questions.modelAnswer: It takes 4200 joules of energy to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of water by 1 °C.

questions.stem: State whether a substance with a low specific heat capacity heats up quickly or slowly, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: It heats up quickly, because only a little energy is needed per kilogram to raise its temperature by each degree.

questions.stem: Explain why the same campfire warms a small iron kettle quickly but a large copper cauldron slowly, even though both metals have low specific heat capacities.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy needed follows ΔQ = mcΔT, so mass matters as well as capacity. The kettle's small mass means the fire supplies its required energy quickly, while the cauldron's much larger mass multiplies the same per-kilogram price into a far larger total demand, so its temperature climbs slowly despite the low specific heat capacity.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg block of a metal with specific heat capacity 420 J/kg °C absorbs 21 000 J from a heater. Calculate its temperature rise.
Which equation gives the change in thermal energy with no change of state?

options.text: ΔQ = m × c ÷ ΔT
options.explanation: The temperature change multiplies; it does not divide.

options.text: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT
options.explanation: Mass times capacity times temperature change.

options.text: ΔQ = m × L
options.explanation: That is the latent heat equation for state changes.

options.text: ΔQ = c × ΔT
options.explanation: The mass factor is missing.

questions.stem: In the equation ΔQ = m × c × ΔT, what are the units of each quantity?

options.text: J, g, J/kg °C, °C
options.explanation: Mass must be in kilograms; grams need converting first.

options.text: J, kg, J/°C, °C
options.explanation: The capacity unit must keep its per-kilogram part.

options.text: J, kg, J/kg °C, °C
options.explanation: Energy, mass, capacity, temperature change — in that order.

options.text: W, kg, J/kg °C, K
options.explanation: ΔQ is energy in joules, not power in watts.

questions.stem: A kettle heats 0.48 kg of water by 0.7 °C. Taking c = 4200 J/kg °C, what energy is transferred?

options.text: about 14 000 J
options.explanation: That overstates the product by a factor of ten.

options.text: about 140 J
options.explanation: That understates the product by a factor of ten.

options.text: about 2016 J
options.explanation: That forgets the 0.7 factor.

options.text: about 1400 J

questions.stem: A student computes a specific heat capacity of 42 000 J/kg °C for water from lab data. The accepted value is 4200. Which error best explains the tenfold result?

options.text: the mass was entered in grams instead of kilograms
options.explanation: c = ΔQ/(mΔT): a mass ten times too big makes c ten times too small — in reverse, an entry slip of units inflates it.

options.text: the temperature change was measured too accurately
options.explanation: Precision does not produce a tenfold bias.

options.text: water's capacity changes with the weather
options.explanation: Water's capacity is effectively constant across lab conditions.

options.text: the accepted value is wrong
options.explanation: 4200 J/kg °C is the established value.

questions.stem: Why does ΔQ = mcΔT give zero energy across a melting plateau, and what replaces it there?

options.text: no energy is supplied during melting
options.explanation: Energy is supplied — it funds the state change.

options.text: ΔT is zero during melting, so latent heat replaces the equation as the energy account
options.explanation: State changes are governed by latent heat, not by ΔQ = mcΔT.

options.text: the mass becomes zero during melting
options.explanation: Mass is conserved through a change of state.

options.text: c becomes infinite during melting
options.explanation: Capacity is defined within a single state.

questions.stem: State the equation linking the thermal energy change to mass, capacity and temperature change.
questions.modelAnswer: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT — change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times change in temperature.

questions.stem: State the rearrangement used to find specific heat capacity from experimental data.
questions.modelAnswer: Divide the measured energy by the product of mass and temperature change: c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT).

questions.stem: Explain why quoting 1411.2 J as 'about 1400 J' is better practice in an exam than leaving the long decimal.
questions.modelAnswer: The inputs — 0.48, 0.7 — carry at most two significant figures, so the product cannot honestly carry more than two. Quoting 1400 J matches the precision of the data, avoids implying a false accuracy, and matches the mark scheme's expectation for rounded final answers.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg block of water-equivalent material at 20 °C is warmed to 50 °C by a 252 000 J input. Show that this is consistent with c = 4200 J/kg °C.
questions.modelAnswer: ΔT = 50 − 20 = 30 °C, so ΔQ = m × c × ΔT = 2.0 × 4200 × 30 = 252 000 J — exactly the supplied energy, confirming the capacity value.
